You do not need to buy a course, open a playing account or finish a reading list to begin. Learn standard no-limit Texas hold’em through one guided hand and six connected stages. Start small, explain a fresh example, then choose the next step. Do one scene or one first-pass lesson, then pause. The reading estimate covers all the explanations and the printable card, rather than the time needed for a single visit.

The guided hand below introduces the action, shared cards and pot in six scenes. Each scene explains an answer and offers a precise repair link. Prefer to read first? Open the first lesson and use its first-pass guide. For smaller steps, learn one idea with a worked example .

Use counters or paper. The actions are scripted to explain the rules and accounting; they are not betting recommendations. Read a scene, give your reason, then compare it with the explanation. You can continue after any answer. Skip to the six-stage lesson map . No account or wager is needed. Six scenes, from the first action to the result.

Six players start with 100 counters each. The small blind posts 1 and the big blind posts 2. There is no ante, fee or side pot. Three players fold. You are on the button, the seat marked by the dealer marker. Both blinds still have their first decisions. First seat: folded Next seat: folded Cutoff: folded Button: you Small blind: posted 1 Big blind: posted 2 Your private cards Shared board No shared cards yet. Pot now 3 Your stack behind 100 Big blind behind 98 After your initial action on the button, who still has an initial decision? Nobody; the flop must come next. The small blind and the big blind. Only the big blind. Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

For this scripted practice hand, you raise to 6 total and the small blind folds. The big blind already posted 2 on this betting round and faces your total wager of 6. The current pot is your 6, the folded small blind's 1 and the big blind's 2: 9. Your private cards Shared board No shared cards yet. Pot now 9 Your stack behind 94 Big blind behind 98 How many additional counters does the big blind need to call? 6 more. 8 more. 4 more. Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

The big blind calls. The flop, the first three shared cards, is jack of spades, seven of hearts and two of hearts. The big blind checks, meaning it makes no bet. Your private cards remain ace of hearts and jack of hearts. Your private cards Shared board Pot now 13 Your stack behind 94 Big blind behind 94 Which description fits your cards on this flop? A pair of jacks and a heart-flush draw. A completed heart flush. Only a draw, with no made hand. Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

The scripted line continues: you bet 4 and the big blind raises to 12 total on the flop. The pot is now the previous 13 plus your 4 plus the opponent's 12: 29. Your preflop contribution belongs to an earlier round. Your private cards Shared board Pot now 29 Your stack behind 90 Big blind behind 82 How many more counters would a flop call add? 12 more. 8 more. 16 more. Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

You call the extra 8. The turn is nine of clubs; both players check, so nobody pays more on that round. The river is four of diamonds, the last shared card. The big blind bets 10 into the pot of 37, making the current pot 47. Your private cards Shared board Pot now 47 Your stack behind 82 Big blind behind 72 Which statement is justified before you decide? You have a heart flush and may check. Your draw can wait for one more community card. You have a pair of jacks; a call would add 10. Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

For the final scripted action, you call 10. The big blind reveals queen of hearts and jack of diamonds. Compare each player's best five. This is one fictional ending, not evidence about how frequently an actual opponent bluffs or bets for value. Your private cards Shared board Opponent at showdown Pot now 57 Your stack behind 72 Big blind behind 72 Which conclusion follows from this ending? You win the pot of 57 and gain 29 overall; that result alone does not grade the earlier call. You make a profit of 57. Winning proves every earlier bet and call was best. Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

This is one route through standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold’em: actions and cards, preflop context, the flop, the river, ranges, then betting purpose. Each lesson begins with a limited first pass. Read those sections, explain the check below without the answer, then use a fresh situation to see what needs repair. The longer examples remain available as references. Use a deck, counters or paper. No wager, playing account or purchase is needed. Begin with stage 1 when everything is new. You can pause anywhere or try the checkpoint first when you already know the mechanics. Need smaller steps? The beginner practice room pairs six short worked examples with 18 changed questions. Start with one skill; use mixed practice later to choose what to revisit. Cards, actions and the pot Learn: read your two cards, distinguish checking from calling, find the player whose turn it is and compare the best five cards. The lesson finishes with a complete hand whose chips reconcile. Before moving on: explain what you owe now, rather than repeating the last number announced. Use only your contribution on this betting round when counting a call. Your starting hand in context Learn: describe position, earlier action, effective stacks and the price before asking whether two cards are worth playing. A hand's label leaves out most of the decision. Before moving on: distinguish information you observed from an assumption about hidden cards. Name who still has a turn, including a player who may raise after your call. Your first decisions after the flop Learn: name the made hand and the draw separately, read checks and raises without inventing the opponent's cards, and notice when a helpful shared card improves the other hand too. Before moving on: explain both what your cards make now and what they still need. A possibility to improve is different from a completed hand or a guaranteed win. The turn, river and showdown Learn: rebuild the hand when a new card arrives, recognize that a missed draw can still have showdown value, and distinguish calling a bluff from making one. On the river there is no further community card to rescue a draw. Before moving on: separate the price of a call from evidence that your hand meets it. Say when the action is complete and whether you are counting outright wins or a share of the pot. Your first range Learn: separate known cards, physically possible hands and assumptions about their frequency. You do not need a chart or percentages for the first pass. Before moving on: name a fact and an assumption separately. A check is an observed action; the opponent’s hidden hand remains unknown. Betting with a purpose Learn: name which worse hands might call a value bet or which better hands might fold to a bluff. Compare a bet with checking when nothing is owed. Before moving on: describe the response you need, rather than using “I have a pair” or “I won the pot” as the whole argument. Keep your place without another account. The website does not save your progress, collect your answers or send a reminder. When a check feels difficult, use its repair link rather than restarting the whole path. When you can explain it, continue to the next stage. After the six stages, try the checkpoint and return later for a fresh explanation. For a guided example and repeated attempts, use the beginner practice room . After the stage you are studying, try its matching checkpoint situation. After all six, choose a pair of unfamiliar situations and explain them with the lesson closed. The aim is to use an idea in a changed setting, rather than recognize a paragraph you just read. Try the beginner checkpoint to see which explanation to revisit. It offers six situations, explanations of common mistakes and six changed situations to retry. Choose two, give your own reason first, then use the exact repair link that fits the difficulty. A familiar-looking answer is more useful when you can explain a new example too. Keep the blank checkpoint workbook (TXT) in your own notes. Record your first reason, one thing you corrected and what happened on the retry. The website does not collect those answers. If wording or navigation still gets in the way, use the optional reader-feedback prompts ; they lead to the existing contact form and explain what it asks for. If you are comfortable with those ideas, you can choose a specific live-play preparation guide or an optional study task below. There is no requirement to start playing for money. At your next study session, close the lesson and try two checkpoint questions before reopening the explanation. Pick different situations on a later day. A possible routine is a short recall check at the next session and another later in the week; this is a practical suggestion, not a tested optimal schedule for poker. Recall: say the rule or question in your own words without looking. Change the example: use the checkpoint’s changed situation, not just the same answer letter. Repair one gap: follow the precise lesson link, then explain the difference. Keep one note: record the skill, the mistake and the link to return to. Pause when the task is done. Use the six-stage study card for your own notes. It includes the route, guided-hand prompts and a later-review plan. Answers and progress are not sent to the website.

The five tasks below are a menu for later study. They are not another beginner course to finish, and the external course is optional. Work at your own pace. A session can be split across several days, repeated, or skipped when you can already do its task. Use a deck on a table, a fictional example or a completed hand. None of these activities requires a wager. Keep two headings in your notes: “What I can now explain” and “What I still need to check.” Those notes are more informative than the number of pages opened. The linked external pages are free to read as listed, although their publishers may also sell products or advertise gambling. 1. Tell the story of one hand. Read one hand from deal to showdown . Then close the page and describe the order: private cards, preflop betting, flop, turn, river and showdown if more than one player remains. Name who still has a decision at each step. Use the official hold'em rules and hand-rankings references below when you get stuck. Your output is a short explanation of a single hand, not a memorized glossary. Before moving on, explain why a hand can finish without anyone showing cards and why winning a pot does not equal gaining that whole amount in profit. 2. Reconstruct a small pot. Use bets, calls and side pots , then write the separate contributions in a fictional heads-up river example. There are 60 chips in the pot before an opponent bets 30. Calling costs another 30, making the final pot 120. With no further betting or fees and ordinary showdown equity, the break-even share is 30 / 120 = 25% . Your task is to label the 60, the opponent's 30 and your additional 30. Do not divide by 90 simply because that is what you can see before calling. The free expected-value article below offers a second explanation. For a longer worked exercise, use the pot-odds workshop . 3. Explain a decision before seeing the ending. Open the river Decision Lab . Before opening the answer panels, write the cost of calling and the assumption about the opponent that would matter most. Then inspect the two endings. Your output is one explanation that distinguishes the decision from its result. You do not have to guess the best action. Finding the missing information is useful. “The opponent could have a bluff” is a possibility, not a measurement of how frequently that opponent bluffs. 4. Choose the kind of poker you want to understand. For live tournaments, use the field guide and identify three event details to confirm. For cash games, read the cash-game study guide and name the relevant costs. For Omaha or a mixed-game broadcast, use the game comparison before judging a showdown. Your output is a statement of the game, betting structure and question. An introductory hold'em rule is not a universal instruction for every game with poker chips. 5. Study one lesson, not an entire archive. MIT's 2016 course page below provides a free university course with video lectures. It is historical teaching material, not a current commercial solver manual. Choose one lesson relevant to your question and note the assumptions behind its examples. The site listing does not mean every video has been watched or every claim independently reproduced. Finish with three sentences: the question, what the lesson helped clarify, and what it did not establish. Keep the next step small using the resource-check sheet . When the lesson is too advanced, return to the specific missing concept instead of concluding you need a more expensive course.

These are complementary starting points, not a ranking. Current listing descriptions, access and review limits come from the same catalogue as the full directory. Prepared with AI assistance. Begin with the goal, card names and a worked five-card hand , then try selecting the cards yourself. Already comfortable with that? Follow the actions in one guided hand . Prefer a reference lesson? Open the first lesson and use its first-pass guide.

You win a hand when every other player folds, or by having the strongest five-card hand among players who reach the showdown. A tied best hand can share the pot. You do not have to bet on every turn to keep playing; the guided hand below explains the actions. A standard deck has 52 different cards: thirteen ranks in each of four suits. The usual high-to-low rank order is A K Q J T 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 . A is ace, K king, Q queen, J jack and T ten. The four suits are spades ♠, hearts ♥, diamonds ♦ and clubs ♣. Suits do not outrank one another. You receive two private cards . The shared board arrives as three cards on the flop, one on the turn, then one on the river. Once all five shared cards are out, choose the strongest five from your seven available cards. Use zero, one or two private cards. An ace can be low in A-2-3-4-5, but a straight cannot wrap through K-A-2-3-4.

Recall: say the rule or question in your own words without looking. Change the example: use the checkpoint’s changed situation, not just the same answer letter. Repair one gap: follow the precise lesson link, then explain the difference. Keep one note: record the skill, the mistake and the link to return to. Pause when the task is done. Use the six-stage study card for your own notes. It includes the route, guided-hand prompts and a later-review plan. Answers and progress are not sent to the website.

The five tasks below are a menu for later study. They are not another beginner course to finish, and the external course is optional. Work at your own pace. A session can be split across several days, repeated, or skipped when you can already do its task. Use a deck on a table, a fictional example or a completed hand. None of these activities requires a wager. Keep two headings in your notes: “What I can now explain” and “What I still need to check.” Those notes are more informative than the number of pages opened. The linked external pages are free to read as listed, although their publishers may also sell products or advertise gambling. 1. Tell the story of one hand. Read one hand from deal to showdown . Then close the page and describe the order: private cards, preflop betting, flop, turn, river and showdown if more than one player remains. Name who still has a decision at each step. Use the official hold'em rules and hand-rankings references below when you get stuck. Your output is a short explanation of a single hand, not a memorized glossary. Before moving on, explain why a hand can finish without anyone showing cards and why winning a pot does not equal gaining that whole amount in profit. 2. Reconstruct a small pot. Use bets, calls and side pots , then write the separate contributions in a fictional heads-up river example. There are 60 chips in the pot before an opponent bets 30. Calling costs another 30, making the final pot 120. With no further betting or fees and ordinary showdown equity, the break-even share is 30 / 120 = 25% . Your task is to label the 60, the opponent's 30 and your additional 30. Do not divide by 90 simply because that is what you can see before calling. The free expected-value article below offers a second explanation. For a longer worked exercise, use the pot-odds workshop . 3. Explain a decision before seeing the ending. Open the river Decision Lab . Before opening the answer panels, write the cost of calling and the assumption about the opponent that would matter most. Then inspect the two endings. Your output is one explanation that distinguishes the decision from its result. You do not have to guess the best action. Finding the missing information is useful. “The opponent could have a bluff” is a possibility, not a measurement of how frequently that opponent bluffs. 4. Choose the kind of poker you want to understand. For live tournaments, use the field guide and identify three event details to confirm. For cash games, read the cash-game study guide and name the relevant costs. For Omaha or a mixed-game broadcast, use the game comparison before judging a showdown. Your output is a statement of the game, betting structure and question. An introductory hold'em rule is not a universal instruction for every game with poker chips. 5. Study one lesson, not an entire archive. MIT's 2016 course page below provides a free university course with video lectures. It is historical teaching material, not a current commercial solver manual. Choose one lesson relevant to your question and note the assumptions behind its examples. The site listing does not mean every video has been watched or every claim independently reproduced. Finish with three sentences: the question, what the lesson helped clarify, and what it did not establish. Keep the next step small using the resource-check sheet . When the lesson is too advanced, return to the specific missing concept instead of concluding you need a more expensive course.

These are complementary starting points, not a ranking. Current listing descriptions, access and review limits come from the same catalogue as the full directory. Prepared with AI assistance. Start with the cards and the goal.

You win a hand when every other player folds, or by having the strongest five-card hand among players who reach the showdown. A tied best hand can share the pot. You do not have to bet on every turn to keep playing; the guided hand below explains the actions.

A standard deck has 52 different cards: thirteen ranks in each of four suits. The usual high-to-low rank order is A K Q J T 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2. A is ace, K king, Q queen, J jack and T ten. The four suits are spades ♠, hearts ♥, diamonds ♦ and clubs ♣. Suits do not outrank one another.

You receive two private cards. The shared board arrives as three cards on the flop, one on the turn, then one on the river. Once all five shared cards are out, choose the strongest five from your seven available cards. Use zero, one or two private cards. An ace can be low in A-2-3-4-5, but a straight cannot wrap through K-A-2-3-4.

What beats what? Open the visual ranking reference

Read strongest to weakest. A royal flush is the highest straight flush. Compare the hand category first, then the relevant ranks and kickers. There is no sixth-card tiebreaker.

  1. Royal flush

    The ace-high straight flush, the highest possible hand.

    A♠K♠Q♠J♠10♠

  2. Straight flush

    Five consecutive ranks in one suit.

    9♥8♥7♥6♥5♥

  3. Four of a kind

    Four equal ranks plus one side card.

    Q♣Q♦Q♥Q♠2♦

  4. Full house

    Three of one rank and two of another.

    J♥J♦J♠4♣4♦

  5. Flush

    Five cards of one suit, not consecutive.

    A♣J♣8♣5♣2♣

  6. Straight

    Five consecutive ranks, not all one suit.

    9♠8♦7♥6♣5♠

  7. Three of a kind

    Three equal ranks and two unmatched side cards.

    8♠8♥8♦K♣3♠

  8. Two pair

    Two different pairs and a side card.

    K♠K♥5♣5♦2♠

  9. One pair

    One pair and three unmatched side cards.

    10♠10♥A♣7♦3♣

  10. High card

    None of the combinations above.

    A♠J♦9♣6♥3♠
